Analysis

Dataset rights should be modeled as a chain of permissions rather than a single badge. The Data Provenance Initiative distinguishes creator-attributable data licenses from code licenses and explicitly limits itself to best-effort self-reported categorization. Common Pile requires confidence that license information originates with a rights holder. These methods support asking who can grant which rights for each component, transformation and release. They do not establish enforceability or replace project-specific legal review.

Evidence: cohort3.claim.provenance.data-license-protocol, cohort3.claim.provenance.scope-caveat, cohort7.claim.commonpile.licensor

Analysis

Web availability and collection permission are distinct. Consent in Crisis reports inconsistencies between robots.txt signals and terms of service in selected corpora. Documenting C4 recommends documenting included and excluded text and leaves some PII/copyright auditing to future work. FineWeb and Dolma acknowledge residual harmful or sensitive content despite filtering. A buyer should retain capture-time permissions, exclusion rules and removal paths, while treating a crawlable page as a source observation rather than automatic authorization to train or redistribute.

Evidence: cohort7.claim.consentcrisis.signals, cohort8.claim.documentingc4.three-views, cohort8.claim.documentingc4.future-audit, candidate.paperfull.fineweb.harmful-content-remains, cohort3.claim.dolma.residual-risk

Analysis

License scope can change within a research artifact. AlpacaEval declares different code and data licenses; RewardBench aggregation remains subject to component terms; MathVista retains original image/question copyright and prohibits training use; GAIA asks against public redistribution. The correct unit for diligence is the exact component and use, not a repository’s top-level license string. A restrictive finding does not imply that this report possesses or can redistribute the underlying data.

Evidence: cohort2.dataset.claim.alpacaeval.component-license, next.claim.rewardbench.terms, cohort4.dataset.claim.mathvista.terms, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.cohort4.dataset.claim.gaia.gate

Analysis

Customer material and website visitor data have different policy boundaries. AfterQuery explicitly excludes processor/service-provider customer processing from its website policy; Mercor excludes its work platform; Label Your Data and LXT describe client-instruction processing; Proximal requires written consent and an executed agreement for generalized-model use of customer material. Obtain the project processing agreement, subprocessors, retention and secondary-use terms. A public policy’s existence does not establish that the proposed delivery is covered by every described safeguard.

Evidence: candidate.cohort4.afterquery.processor-privacy-boundary, candidate.supplier.mercor.privacy-scope, repair20261111.claim.current-reference138, candidate.cohort2.lxt.processor-scope, candidate.cohort4.proximal.customer-material-training-consent

Source-backed finding

Entity names and terms require exact scope. Kili’s May 2025 legal notice names MYAI SAS, while its same-date EULA names KILI-TECHNOLOGY SAS under the same Paris registration number; the public inconsistency is unresolved. DDD’s published Terms of Use name DDD Ventures LLC and use investment/real-estate language, so that page does not settle the AI-data contracting identity. iSoftStone’s privacy policy identifies a website-scoped US operator without resolving ultimate ownership or group-wide contracting responsibility. These findings preserve uncertainty rather than invent corporate transactions or additional suppliers.

Evidence: candidate.cohort6.kili_technology.published-operator-name, candidate.cohort6.digital_divide_data.legal-page-discrepancy, candidate.cohort6.isoftstone.website-operator

Analysis

Secondary use and human access can be explicit commercial conditions. Datasaur’s terms contain a free-access deidentified/aggregate improvement exception; Deploy’s terms default to manual Hive Worker review of customer content unless otherwise agreed in writing; Dataocean’s website policy leaves product/project rules to the corresponding services. None of these clauses alone establishes what happened to a particular customer’s records. A buyer should identify the applicable subscription, written exceptions, worker exposure, use permissions and service-specific privacy terms before choosing a delivery path.

Evidence: candidate.cohort6.datasaur.customer-data-use-scope, candidate.cohort6.hive.manual-review-default, candidate.cohort6.speechocean.website-privacy-scope

Source-backed finding

Toloka’s published task guidelines distinguish public-space images, third-party personal information and personal information collected from Tolokers. For third-party information, the listed conditions include both anonymization before upload and consent agreements. Collection from Tolokers also carries lawful-collection, administering-entity, purpose and policy conditions. These are category-specific platform rules, not a finding that every dataset complies. The linked additional collection guidelines were not separately captured in the reviewed scope.

Evidence: candidate.supplier.toloka.pii-rules

Analysis

Biometric and authorship metadata deserve separate consent and use records. Toloka’s notice bases identity matching on explicit consent and says refusal can prevent onboarding; it also discloses authorship metadata in some coding deliverables. Turing’s policy lists AI development/training uses of personal information, while Polymath excludes interview voice recordings and transcripts from model training. These statements concern different records and services. Preserve which person, purpose, data type and downstream use each notice covers rather than combine them into a general permission claim.

Evidence: candidate.supplier.toloka.biometric-consent, candidate.supplier.toloka.client-code-metadata, candidate.supplier.turing.personal-data-ai-use, candidate.cohort4.polymath_ai_labs.interview-training-restriction

Analysis

Security disclosure must retain attestation type and scope. Scale states SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO/IEC 27001:2022; Appen describes SOC 2 Type II, a HIPAA-specific solution and facility options; Snorkel states SOC 2 Type 2 and engagement-start scoping; Prolific describes ISO 27001 and Cyber Essentials while treating SOC 2 Type 2 as a future plan. Underlying reports, certificate scopes and customer deployments were not inspected here. These statements should not be flattened into equivalent independently verified controls.

Evidence: candidate.supplier.scale_ai.security-disclosure, repair20261111.claim.current-reference078, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.candidate.supplier.snorkel_ai.security-scope, candidate.supplier.prolific.security

Analysis

Operational controls can be tiered or project-specific. CloudFactory distinguishes included network controls from optional endpoint controls; Sama describes assigned-employee project rooms; Encord describes role permissions; DataForce’s vendor notice requires an applicable DPA before EU-personal-data processing. A buyer should verify the selected tier, location, legal entity, access matrix and actual data flow. The report records disclosed controls, without certifying that all personnel or projects implement them.

Evidence: candidate.cohort2.cloudfactory.network-baseline, candidate.cohort2.cloudfactory.endpoint-controls, repair20261111.claim.current-reference094, candidate.cohort3.encord.access-roles, candidate.cohort2.dataforce.vendor-dpa

Analysis

Incidents and remediation should be compared on evidence, not on whether one company has a public disclosure. Mercor’s company investigation account describes the March 2026 compromised LiteLLM event and is explicitly not an independently audited impact/remediation finding. This report has no common incident-discovery process or equal disclosure window across suppliers. It therefore cannot rank relative security from the presence of that one record or assume that an unrecorded incident never occurred elsewhere.

Evidence: candidate.supplier.mercor.incident

Analysis

Artifact attribution is nontransitive. Scale’s HelpSteer annotation, Translated’s multilingual role, Prolific’s recruitment case, Toloka’s U-MATH validation and Surge’s GSM8K collection are specific relationships. A paper citing a dataset, an author’s affiliation, a supplier’s general service menu or a benchmark family’s parent link does not establish another supplier contribution. The graph is sparse in explicit object relationships; many approved observations are typed text. A reader should not confuse catalogue richness with an exhaustive supplier-to-artifact map.

Evidence: candidate.supplier.scale_ai.helpsteer3-contribution, next.claim.helpsteer3.translated, candidate.supplier.prolific.cohere-recruitment, candidate.supplier.toloka.umath-validation, candidate.supplier.surge_ai.gsm8k-contribution

Method

Research governance: the publisher’s public identity discloses applications for paid work at some covered companies, membership in A.Team’s talent network and a separate proposed AI research lab. No profiled company has paid for coverage or is a customer, investor or affiliate of the publisher under that disclosure. External reviewer credit requires consent. This preparation claims actual separate AI source review and will require separate exact-report evidence-auditor and adversarial review; it does not claim human peer review or an external operational certification.

Research gap

Governance unknowns include project-specific contracts, current assurance-report scopes, removal-request outcomes, consent withdrawals, subprocessor execution and worker appeal effectiveness. These cannot be resolved by treating a top-level license, policy statement or source-content review as an operational audit. Buyer diligence should obtain the relevant documents and test the actual project boundary; future research should record both support and unresolved limitations.

Analysis

Disclosure completeness is an observable governance input, while actual conduct remains a separate question. GIGO audits publication reporting in a selected literature; Who Annotates extracts task-level disclosures with an automated model and a separately adjudicated reference. Both reject equating missing reporting with absent practice. Their results justify asking for training, language proficiency, instructions and reconciliation records. They do not justify ranking a supplier’s ethics or data quality from how many public fields are filled.

Evidence: cohort9.claim.gigo.audit-limit, cohort9.claim.gigo.instructions, cohort9.claim.whoannotates.task-level-audit, cohort9.claim.whoannotates.adjudication, cohort9.claim.whoannotates.reporting-pattern, cohort9.claim.whoannotates.audit-limit

Analysis

A documented consent workflow does not finish privacy diligence. WildChat reports an agreement plus secondary confirmation and multilingual PII filtering, yet warns that hashed IPs and request headers can link conversations. The reported process was not independently tested here. For a proposed conversational-data use, examine the exact released fields, linkage routes, permissions and intended population; preserve the difference between a source’s stated control and demonstrated residual risk reduction.

Evidence: cohort9.claim.wildchat.consent-gate, cohort9.claim.wildchat.anonymization, cohort9.claim.wildchat.selection-limit

Analysis

Public availability and private evaluation are separate diligence questions. Riemann-Bench is private; APEX-Accounting distinguishes private tasks and a small public development world; ALE has unresolved public-instance count wording; DAYJOB evaluates more finance tasks than its public finance release. None of these facts alone invalidates the scientific use, but each changes independent reproducibility and a buyer’s access obligation. Confidence is high in this distinction. Require a precise access manifest, permitted reproduction scope and complete task/attempt accounting; inspected payloads and executable grading checks would change reproducibility confidence.

Evidence: repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.limitation, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.method, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.result, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.limitation, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.method, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.result, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v2.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2606.05405.limitation, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v2.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2606.05405.method, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v2.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2606.05405.result, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2610.01306.limitation, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2610.01306.method, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2610.01306.result

Analysis

Rights evidence should follow each component. A paper’s benchmark declaration does not establish rights to every included chart, source image, copied repository or professional document. StarCoder explicitly retains license/opt-out detection limits; Chartography’s online provenance does not establish chart redistribution rights; the new VQA family reports a creator CC-BY release statement without a per-image audit. Confidence is high in the need to keep those scopes separate and unestablished for any particular buyer’s legal permission. Obtain governing release instruments and component-level provenance rather than convert source review into a rights certification.

Evidence: mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.limitation, mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.main_result, mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.method, mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.provenance, mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.result, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2608.10677.limitation, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2608.10677.method, repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2608.10677.result, candidate.mandatory19.benchmark.hf.toloka.wsdmcup2023.crowd-construction, candidate.mandatory19.benchmark.hf.toloka.wsdmcup2023.iou-protocol-and-baseline, candidate.mandatory19.benchmark.hf.toloka.wsdmcup2023.overlap-and-mirror-identity, candidate.mandatory19.benchmark.hf.toloka.wsdmcup2023.release-license-scope, candidate.mandatory19.benchmark.hf.toloka.wsdmcup2023.split-and-instance-units

Analysis

Versioned rights comparison — permission statements attach to different objects. GeneBench-Pro’s preprint carries CC-BY-NC 4.0 while its public case-study package declares MIT; CVDP separates non-code, original code and upstream components with two unspecified NOTICE entries; DeepResearch Bench II distinguishes evaluation code from task-specific licenses and later generated model reports. Confidence is high in keeping those declarations separate and unestablished for a buyer’s exact downstream grant. Build a component-and-use schedule with source documents and obtain the applicable instruments. A verified exact payload and rights chain would change the assessment; the synthesis itself grants no source-corpus rights.

Analysis

A benchmark-use instruction can coexist with a permissive metadata license. GDP.xlsx preserves an Apache label beside directions excluding training and checkpoint selection. µ-MATH separates model-output license terms from other fields. AA-LCR licenses its questions while declining to claim rights over accompanying document text, and the Nexdata listings describe paid commercial access whose terms depend on the project. These observations support a component-and-use matrix covering questions, source media, traces, annotations, code and execution environments. They do not provide a legal reconciliation or blanket permission. Confidence is high in the disclosed scope distinctions; a rights judgment would require the actual applicable terms and permissions.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.gdp-xlsx.use-constraints.v2, candidate.normal12.mu-math.license-scope.v2, candidate.third11.aa-lcr.license.v2, candidate.add17.nexdata2121.access.v2

Analysis

Declared privacy and synthetic fixtures should be reported at the object actually described. EMRBench’s fixture is described as synthetic; RedlineBench describes fictional parties and scrubbed metadata; Nexdata’s hand-pose listing says facial-identifying information is absent. None of these observations is an independent consent, reidentification or downstream-use audit. The reasoning is to request a data-flow and provenance record for each delivered component rather than infer complete privacy protection from a category label. Confidence is high in preserving these public-source limits and unmeasured in any private payload’s actual properties. An authorized component-level inspection and project-specific provenance evidence could narrow those unknowns.

Evidence: candidate.next12.emrbench.synthetic-fixture.v2, candidate.third11.redlinebench.release.v2, candidate.add17.nexdata1463.fields.v2
